query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Processing a Ti–Ni primary HEA via direct energy deposition (DED) with optimized high cooling-rate parameters (e.g., laser power ~300 W and scanning speed ~800 mm/s) followed by a brief stress-relief heat treatment will refine the microstructure and enhance its elevated-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: A Ti–Ni primary HEA produced via conventional processing that exhibits coarse grains, local segregation, and associated elevated-temperature performance limitations.
generation.intervention: Employ DED additive manufacturing with tightly controlled processing parameters (high cooling rates approximating 10⁴ K/s) and subsequently apply a brief stress-relief heat treatment (e.g., 600 °C for 15 minutes).
generation.conditions: Manufacture under DED conditions using optimized laser settings in an inert atmosphere; minimal post-processing aside from the stress relief; mechanical testing performed at temperatures up to ~1100 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, homogeneous grain structure with reduced segregation and lower defect density, coupled with mitigated residual stresses.
generation.mechanism: Rapid solidification during DED produces a much finer microstructure and uniform elemental distribution. The short stress-relief treatment minimizes residual stresses without significantly coarsening the grains, thereby enhancing grain boundary strengthening and overall mechanical performance at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: A moderate improvement in high-temperature yield strength, ductility, and creep resistance compared to conventionally processed samples, with expected quantitative gains on the order of 15–20%.
generation.baseline: Conventionally processed Ti–Ni HEAs exhibit coarser grains and minor segregation defects that limit the effectiveness of high-temperature strengthening mechanisms.
generation.boundary: The benefits depend on maintaining high cooling rates and effective stress-relief without inducing additional defects; applicable for operational temperatures up to ~1100 °C with compositions within standard HEA compositional ranges.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the precise DED processing window and stress-relief parameters needed to optimize microstructure without introducing detrimental residual stresses or defects; scaling to industrial production may require further optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate Ti–Ni HEA samples via conventional processing and via optimized DED processing (with specified laser power, scanning speed, and post-process stress relief). Characterize the microstructure (grain size, homogeneity, residual stress) and compare high-temperature mechanical performance via tensile and creep tests.
measurements: Grain size and defect density measurements (SEM/TEM, XRD residual stress analysis)
High-temperature tensile strength and ductility data
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the DED-processed samples, after stress relief, do not exhibit a statistically significant refinement of the microstructure and a corresponding improvement (approximately 15–20% or more) in high-temperature mechanical properties relative to conventional samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) have drawn significant attention due to their unique design and superior mechanical properties. Comprising 5–35 at% of five or more elements with similar atomic radii, HEAs exhibit high configurational entropy, resulting in single-phase solid solutions rather than intermetallic compounds. Additive manufacturing (AM), particularly direct energy deposition (DED), is effective for producing HEAs due to its rapid cooling rates, which ensure uniform microstructures and minimize defects. These alloys typically form face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) structures, contributing to their exceptional strength, hardness, and mechanical performance across various temperatures. However, FCC-structured HEAs often have low yield strengths, posing a challenge for structural applications. In this study, a Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA was manufactured using the DED method. This study proposes that the addition of aluminum and titanium creates a γ + γ′ phase structure within a multicomponent FCC-HEA matrix, enhancing the thermal stability and coarsening the resistance and strength. In particular, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are the HEAs based on refractory materials such as Ti [], V [], Cr [], Zr [], Hf [], Nb [], Mo [], Ta [], W [], and Mn [], which have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures. RHEAs have a crystal structure such as FCC, FCC+BCC, and BCC phases, a microstructure including a precipitated phase, and intermetallic compounds such as the BCC B2 phase and Laves phase []. Most research using HEAs was conducted during evaluation of the basic properties by manufacturing ingots using arc melting and casting []. The conventional casting method of manufacturing HEAs has the problem of difficulty in forming a single-phase solid solution due to a low cooling rate. As the size of the manufactured HEA increases, it is difficult to secure the uniformity of the microstructure because the internal cooling rate and the external cooling rate are different. The non-uniformed microstructure causes degradation and non-uniformity of the mechanical properties of the HEAs [,].
